A skew-symmetric matrix has zeros on its diagonal, and each entry above the diagonal fixes its mirror entry below, so the free entries are the n(n-1)/2 slots strictly above the diagonal.
The entries on and above the diagonal can be chosen freely, with every entry below determined by the negation rule, so the number of free parameters is n(n+1)/2.
Rewriting AB = I as AB - I = 0 and factoring the left side as B times (A - I) leaves a product equal to zero, and for a general A that forces B itself to vanish.
For square matrices, AB = I forces det(A) times det(B) to equal 1, so A is invertible, B has to be its inverse, and an inverse works from both sides, giving BA = I.
